lessons.title: How doctors assess possible PsA
pages: There is no single test for PsA. A doctor looks at the whole pattern. This is often a rheumatologist, a doctor for joint and immune system diseases. They ask about your symptoms. They ask if psoriasis or PsA runs in your family. They check your joints, skin, and nails. Swollen or tender joints, psoriasis, and nail changes are important signs.

Blood tests help rule out other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis. X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI can show changes in joints, the spine, or where tendons attach to bone. See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back. Bring a short list of your changes to the visit.
key_takeaways: There is no single test for PsA.
See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back.

lines.text: Hi there, and welcome! Today, let’s find out how doctors check for possible psoriatic arthritis, or PsA.
See a doctor if you have joint pain, stiffness, and swelling that keeps coming back.
Go even if you do not have psoriasis. These symptoms need to be checked.
If your doctor thinks you may have PsA, they will send you to a specialist called a rheumatologist.
A rheumatologist is a doctor who treats joint and immune system diseases.
There is no single test that can prove you have PsA.
Instead, the doctor puts several clues together: your story, an exam, and some tests.
First, the doctor talks with you about your symptoms.
For example, PsA symptoms can be worse first thing in the morning, and may get better with exercise.
The doctor will ask if anyone in your family has psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis.
PsA can sometimes start after a person has had psoriasis for many years.
Next comes a physical exam.
Swollen or tender joints, psoriasis on the skin, and nail changes are important signs.
If you have never been told you have psoriasis, the doctor may check your skin for it.
PsA can affect the joints, the spine, the skin, and the nails.
It can also affect places where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone, like the back of the heel.
Some people get a whole finger or toe that swells up, like a little sausage.
Nail changes can include tiny dents, called pitting, or a nail that lifts away from the skin underneath.
A blood test helps check for other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis.
Other conditions can also cause joint pain, stiffness, and swelling. Examples are osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and gout.
Sometimes, a little fluid is taken from a sore joint and tested.
X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI scans can show changes in the joints, the spine, or where tendons attach to bone.
Each test is just one clue.
The doctor looks at all the clues together to see the whole pattern.
It pays to be prepared.
Problems like a delay in diagnosis can happen, unless we plan ahead.
So bring a short list of your changes, even if they come and go. And note how long stiffness lasts after you wake up.
Great job! Let’s review.
There is no single test for PsA.
Your doctor puts together your story, an exam, and tests.
See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back.

lessons.title: Understanding the CASPAR framework
pages: CASPAR is a set of rules doctors use to classify PsA. First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment. Then other signs are added. Psoriasis you have now counts the most. Psoriasis in the past, or in your family, also counts.

Nail changes count. So does a whole finger or toe that is swollen, now or in the past. A negative test for rheumatoid factor (RF) counts. So does new bone next to a joint on an X-ray. A heel spur alone does not count. A score is not a home diagnosis.
key_takeaways: First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment.
A score is not a home diagnosis.

lines.text: Hi again! Let’s learn about CASPAR.
CASPAR stands for Classification criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis.
It comes from a study published in 2006.
Doctors use it to sort the signs of PsA into groups.
Step one is a must.
There has to be inflammation in a joint, in the spine, or where a tendon attaches to bone.
Step two adds points for other signs.
There are five groups of signs.
Group one is psoriasis.
Psoriasis on your skin or scalp right now counts the most.
If you don’t have it now, having had it in the past counts. If you never had it, psoriasis in a close family member counts.
Group two is nail changes you have now.
Examples are tiny dents called pitting, a nail lifting off the skin underneath, or thick buildup under the nail.
Group three is a blood test called rheumatoid factor, or RF.
Here, a negative result is the one that counts.

scenes.name: Group 4: A swollen finger or toe

lines.text: Group four is a whole finger or toe that is swollen, sometimes called a sausage digit.
It counts if it is swollen now, or if a doctor wrote it down in the past.

scenes.name: Group 5: New bone on an X-ray

lines.text: Group five is new bone forming right next to a joint, seen on an X-ray.
A heel spur alone is not that finding.

scenes.name: Points are not a home test

lines.text: The reference adds up these points.
But a score is not a home diagnosis.
A doctor must look at all the findings and check for other causes.
Knowing CASPAR can help you follow the conversation with your care team.

lessons.title: What PsA is
pages: Psoriatic arthritis, or PsA, is a long-term condition linked to inflammation. The immune system becomes overactive. This can cause pain and swelling in joints and where tendons attach to bone. Psoriasis is a related skin condition that can cause scaly patches. Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition. Many people have skin psoriasis before joint symptoms begin. Some notice joint symptoms first.

The next lesson groups PsA into six areas, called domains. These are skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, swollen fingers or toes, and tendon attachment sites. You may have changes in some areas and not others. Not everyone has changes in all six areas. Skin and joint changes may follow different patterns. These areas describe the disease. They are not the six topics in this course.
key_takeaways: Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition.
Not everyone has changes in all six areas.

lines.text: Hi there! In this lesson, let’s find out what psoriatic arthritis, or PsA, really is.
PsA is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in the joints, and in the places where tendons and ligaments attach to bone.
Those attachment places are called entheses.
In PsA, the immune system becomes overactive, for reasons no one fully understands.
This creates inflammation, which leads to pain and swelling.
Psoriasis is a related skin condition that can cause scaly patches.
Most people with PsA already have psoriasis when they are diagnosed.
On average, PsA starts about 7 to 10 years after skin symptoms begin.
But a small group of people notice joint pain before any skin rash.
So psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition.
Anyone can get PsA. It is most common in adults, and it affects men and women equally.
Genes play a part. Many people with PsA have family members with the disease.
Things like obesity, infection, injury, or stress may help trigger it.
Doctors group PsA into six areas, called domains.
They are skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, swollen fingers or toes, and tendon attachment sites.
You may have changes in some areas and not others. Not everyone has all six.
Symptoms vary a lot from person to person.
There is no cure yet, but treatment can slow the disease, ease pain, and protect your joints.
Early treatment is linked to better results, and less damage.
Great job! Let’s review.
Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition.
Not everyone has changes in all six areas.

lessons.title: PsA across the body
pages: The six card labels describe different parts of PsA. Skin psoriasis means scaly skin patches. Nail psoriasis can cause pits or lifting of the nail. Peripheral arthritis affects joints away from the spine, such as those in the hands or knees. Axial disease affects the spine and may involve the joints that join the spine to the pelvis. These are called sacroiliac, or SI, joints.

Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe. Enthesitis means inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. The back or bottom of the heel may be affected. These six domains can help guide treatment discussions. They do not name a drug that is right for you. Eye or bowel inflammation can also occur alongside PsA. These are separate from the six domains. Heart health, blood sugar, weight, and mood can also matter in care. The symptoms topic covers these concerns and changes over time.
key_takeaways: Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe.
These six domains can help guide treatment discussions.

lines.text: Welcome back! Let’s take a tour of the six areas of PsA.
First, skin psoriasis: raised, scaly patches on the skin.
They often show up on the scalp, the elbows, or the knees.
Second, nail psoriasis.
Nails can get tiny dents called pits, crumble, or lift away from the nail bed.
Third, peripheral arthritis. This means joints away from the spine, like the hands or the knees.
Joints may feel stiff, painful, or swollen. Stiffness is often worse in the morning, or after resting.
Fourth, axial disease. This affects the spine, and may involve the sacroiliac, or SI, joints, where the spine meets the pelvis.
It can cause stiffness in the neck, the lower back, and the hips.
Fifth, dactylitis: a whole finger or toe that swells up, like a little sausage.
It can be painful.
Sixth, enthesitis: inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone.
The back of the heel and the sole of the foot are common spots.
These six domains can help guide treatment talks with your team.
But they do not name a drug that is right for you.
Eye or bowel inflammation can also happen alongside PsA.
Eye inflammation, called uveitis, must be treated quickly to avoid vision loss.
These are separate from the six domains.
People with PsA also have a higher risk of other health conditions, like heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.
Mood matters, too.
Treating PsA well can lower the risk of some of these.
Nice work! Let’s review.
Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe.
These six domains can help guide treatment discussions.

lessons.title: Eyes and symptoms that need prompt care
pages: The eyes card describes inflammation inside the eye. One name for this is uveitis. It can cause eye pain, redness, blurred sight, or trouble with bright light. These symptoms can have other causes, too. A body map cannot tell which cause is present.

New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Possible acute eye inflammation needs a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. Do not wait for your next routine visit or a reply in the app. An eye exam is needed to find the cause.
key_takeaways: A body map cannot tell which cause is present.
Seek emergency care for a loss of vision.

lines.text: This lesson is about your eyes. It is short, but very important.
Sometimes, inflammation can happen inside the eye. One name for this is uveitis.
It usually affects one eye, but it can affect both.
Signs include eye pain, red or watery eyes, blurred vision, and being bothered by bright light.
Some people also see flashes, or floating dark spots.
Symptoms can come on quickly, over hours or days, or more slowly, over weeks.
These symptoms can have other causes, too.
A body map cannot tell which cause is present.
New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment, the same day.
Do not wait for your next routine visit, or a reply in the app.
Seek emergency care for any loss of vision.
An eye specialist can find the cause and start treatment quickly.
Treating it early helps prevent long-term problems, like vision loss.
It usually gets better with treatment, but it can come back.
Great job! Let’s review.
A body map cannot tell which cause is present.

lessons.title: Related health and changes over time
pages: The statement above the body map says PsA may lead to lasting damage. Disease activity can rise and fall. A flare is a time when symptoms return or worsen. A flare and lasting joint damage are different. A flare describes activity now; damage refers to changes that may persist. There is no fixed sequence that everyone follows. Treatment aims to control symptoms and limit harm. Tell the team about changes in pain, swelling, fatigue, or daily tasks.

A comorbidity means another health condition alongside PsA. This is not the same as joint damage. Your team may discuss heart health, blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, weight, or mood. Some people also have eye or bowel inflammation. Ask which health checks fit your history. A higher risk does not mean you will get another condition. A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk. Share concerns so the care plan can address your whole health.
key_takeaways: A flare and lasting joint damage are different.
A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk.

lines.text: Let’s talk about how PsA can change over time, and about your whole health.
PsA inflammation may lead to lasting damage if it is not treated.
Treatment can slow the disease and protect your joints.
Disease activity can rise and fall.
A flare is a time when symptoms come back, or get worse.
A flare and lasting joint damage are different.
A flare describes activity now. Damage means changes that may stay.
Flares should not happen often when your disease is treated well.
If flares happen often, talk with your provider about changing your plan.
There is no fixed path that everyone follows.
Tell your team about changes in pain, swelling, tiredness, or daily tasks.
A comorbidity means another health condition alongside PsA.
These can include high blood pressure, high blood sugar, high cholesterol, heart disease, weight, and low mood.
Some of these may have no symptoms you notice, so regular check-ups with your primary care provider matter.
Caught early, many can be treated with lifestyle changes or medicine.
Having a higher risk does not mean you will get another condition.
And a number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk.
Ask which health checks fit your history, and share your concerns.
Great job! Let’s review.
A flare and lasting joint damage are different.
A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk.

lessons.title: Gut and bowel changes
pages: The gut card describes pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD, can occur alongside PsA. This is a condition that causes inflammation in the gut. A bowel change does not prove that you have IBD or that PsA is the cause.

Tell your care team about gut symptoms that keep happening. Note what changed, when it started, and how it affects your day. Your team may ask about your medicines and decide whether you need more tests. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help.
key_takeaways: A bowel change does not prove that you have IBD or that PsA is the cause.
Tell your care team about gut symptoms that keep happening.

lessons.title: Wrists, hands, fingers, and nails
pages: This card groups several changes in the hands. A wrist or finger joint may hurt, swell, or feel stiff. Swelling of a whole finger is called dactylitis. It is different from swelling around just one joint. These changes can make tasks such as holding a cup or using buttons harder.

Nail psoriasis may cause small pits, yellow spots, or a nail lifting from its bed. The photo shows examples of nail changes. Nail changes and joint symptoms do not always happen together. Tell your team whether the change is in a nail, a joint, or the whole finger. Mention any trouble with daily tasks.

lessons.title: Understanding treatment groups
pages: Medicines have different jobs. Some help ease pain and swelling. Others aim to control the disease process. These are called DMARDs. Conventional DMARDs act broadly on the immune system. Biologic drugs target selected immune signals. Targeted synthetic drugs act on pathways inside cells. These are names for groups. They do not rank drugs from good to bad. Some drugs are pills. lessons.title: The four pillars of daily care
pages: Four pillars can help organize daily life with arthritis: Nourishment, Motion, Mastery, and Repose. In plain words, these mean food, movement, coping, and rest. They are a way to plan a discussion about everyday needs. They do not replace medical treatment. This framework is a guide to daily habits. It is not a test of how well your disease is controlled.

Think about which part of daily life is hardest right now. Food choices, activity, mood, and sleep may each raise different questions. A practical plan can focus on a small change that fits your needs and abilities. The care team can help tailor it. Bring up barriers such as pain, cost, fatigue, or poor sleep. Daily care works best as part of a shared plan, rather than as a test of willpower. Start with one small step you choose with your team. For example, plan a short walk that fits your joints, or set aside time to wind down before bed. Notice how the step fits into your day. You can adjust it as your needs change.
key_takeaways: They do not replace medical treatment.

They are a way to plan a talk about everyday needs.
They do not replace medical treatment.
The pillars work best together. Each one supports the others.
For example, better sleep can give you more energy to move, and a calmer mind can make healthy habits easier.
This framework is a guide to daily habits.
It is not a test of how well your disease is controlled.
Think about which part of daily life is hardest right now.
Bring up barriers, like pain, cost, tiredness, or poor sleep.
Start small. Small, steady steps add up over time.
For example, a short walk that fits your joints, or time to wind down before bed.
Daily care works best as part of a shared plan, not as a test of willpower.
Your care team can help tailor it, and you can adjust it as your needs change.
Great job! Let’s review.
They do not replace medical treatment.
The care team can help tailor it.

lessons.title: Movement, coping, and support
pages: Motion means finding ways to move that fit your joints and current health. Activity plans may include gentle movement, strength, and daily tasks. A physical therapist can help adapt a plan when pain or reduced movement gets in the way. An occupational therapist can suggest ways to protect joints during tasks. Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change. Walking, swimming, or cycling may be options. Ask your team which activities fit you before you start. The source also describes strength work and tai chi. You do not need to try every type of exercise.

Mastery means building ways to cope with the demands of a long-term condition. It does not mean controlling every symptom by thinking differently. Pain, fatigue, and uncertainty can affect mood and confidence. Support from trusted people, a support group, or a trained counselor may help. Tell the care team when worry or low mood affects daily life. Asking for support is part of care, not a sign of failure. A quiet pause or slow breathing may help you make space for stress. These are coping tools. They do not mean that pain is your fault or that you should skip medical care.
key_takeaways: Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change.
Asking for support is part of care, not a sign of failure.
lessons.review_notes: General movement and coping education only; no exercise dose, activity target, or claim that stress control treats PsA.

lines.text: Let’s talk about moving your body, coping with stress, and getting support.
Motion means finding ways to move that fit your joints, and your current health.
Low-impact activities, like walking, cycling, swimming, yoga, or tai chi, may be especially helpful.
Talk with your doctor before starting any exercise program.
Water can take weight off sore joints while you move.
A stationary bike supports your weight, and you can keep the resistance low.
Strength work, with your body weight, bands, or light weights, builds muscle that supports your joints.
You do not need to try every type of exercise.
A physical therapist can help improve how your joints work.
An occupational therapist can teach ways to protect your joints and save energy.
Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change.

Practices like slow breathing, a quiet pause, or a body scan may help you make space for stress.
These are coping tools. They do not mean that pain is your fault.

lessons.title: Food, sleep, and recovery
pages: Nourishment focuses on food and nutrition needs. Food choices need to fit your own health and life. Food does not replace your prescribed PsA care. A dietitian can help with choices that fit your health, budget, and preferences. Ask about supplements or major diet changes before adding them to your care plan. The food chapter discusses vegetables, fruit, and sources of protein. Use these as topics to discuss with your team. It does not mean one food can switch off PsA. The lesson does not ask you to fast or follow a strict diet.

Repose focuses on rest and sleep. Pain or worry may make sleep harder, and poor sleep can make the next day feel harder to manage. Bring ongoing sleep problems to the care team. Describe whether pain, waking at night, or daytime tiredness is the main concern. Plans for meals, movement, coping, and rest should fit together. The aim is a manageable routine, rather than a strict rule for every day. Try to keep a steady time for bed and waking. A quiet, dark room and a calm wind-down routine may help. Let the team know if pain keeps waking you. Ask for help with sleep rather than changing your medicine on your own.
key_takeaways: Food does not replace your prescribed PsA care.
Bring ongoing sleep problems to the care team.
lessons.review_notes: General framework only. Fasting, elimination diets, alcohol advice, supplement doses, and disease-treatment claims are omitted.

lessons.title: Sharing changes with your care team
pages: Tell the care team about symptoms that are new, keep returning, or are getting worse. A body map can help you name the area: skin, nails, hands, wrists, shoulders, elbows, back, hips, knees, ankles, or feet. Mention fatigue and changes in walking, sleep, work, or self-care. A useful message says where the problem is, when it began, and what has changed. You can say, for example, that new knee pain makes stairs harder.

A body map cannot tell you how urgent a symptom is. The next lesson explains eye and gut changes to report. Medicine concerns and repeated flares are also reasons to contact the prescribing team. Ask your clinic for its phone number and office hours. Ask about expected response times and how to get help when it is closed. Keep your own care plan available. For urgent symptoms, use urgent medical services rather than waiting for a routine app message.
key_takeaways: A useful message says where the problem is, when it began, and what has changed.
A body map cannot tell you how urgent a symptom is.
lessons.review_notes: The supplied May 2019 PsA/AS poster supports naming symptom locations and talking with a healthcare provider. It does not define urgency, distinguish causes, or provide an ACCR protocol. No invented local contacts or response times.

Tell your care team about symptoms that are new, keep coming back, or are getting worse.
A body map can help you name the area: skin, nails, hands, wrists, shoulders, elbows, back, hips, knees, ankles, or feet.
Also mention tiredness, and changes in walking, sleep, work, or self-care.

lessons.title: Eye and gut changes to report
pages: Eye symptoms can need prompt attention. New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Guidance for possible acute eye inflammation calls for a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. These symptoms have several possible causes. An examination is needed to find the cause; the app cannot diagnose uveitis from symptoms.

Tell the care team about ongoing gut pain, bloating, or changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease can occur alongside PsA, but a bowel change does not prove that it is the cause. Describe what changed and when. Your team can decide whether another assessment is needed. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help. Do not wait for a routine visit to discuss an urgent eye problem.
key_takeaways: New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment.
Seek emergency care for a loss of vision.
lessons.review_notes: Generic urgency education based on NHS/NICE, adapted without UK telephone numbers. ACCR clinical review and local routing are still required.
